newsitem.title: ITALY: Justice system overhaul on agenda at Italy cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Justice system overhaul on agenda at Italy cabinet.

text.p: Italy's cabinet will discuss new- style plea bargaining, swifter trials and other reforms on Friday to try to speed up a justice system creaking under the weight of graft investigations.
A government statement on Thursday said ministers would discuss the 43 pages of proposals at a morning meeting.
Once approved by the centre-left government, the package will go to parliament for debate.

The crux of the package, drafted by Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick, is a plan to allow plea bargaining for all crimes where the maximum sentence is three years. Murder, Mafia activities, kidnapping, sexual violence and drug trafficking would all be exempt.

Many commentators have argued that the new-look penal system would provide a way of closing the chapter on the Tangentopoli (Bribesville) scandals which broke in 1992, unleashing a torrent of investigations into corruption in public life.

A judicial war on graft swept the political old guard from power and put prominent figures including former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, Cesare Romiti, boss of carmaker Fiat and top Italian fashion designers on trial.
Flick's package, which has been revised slightly since details emerged last weekend, has been broadly welcomed by magistrates struggling with Italy's tortuously slow system.
Several hundred Tangentopoli cases have yet to come to court. Legal experts say many could lapse under a statute of limitation unless action is taken to clear the backlog.
Under Flick's proposals, defendants could seek a trial under the new plea-bargain system which could spare them jail.
Plea-bargaining has been allowed in Italy only since 1990 and is limited to a relatively small number of cases.

Flick, who is a trained lawyer, had wanted defendants to plead guilty in order to qualify but the stipulation was criticised by constitutional experts as a kind of legal blackmail. He is now proposing that the confession clause will be at the court's discretion.
The proposals would allow judges to impose community service or house arrest instead of jail terms on those who take the new plea-bargain and speedy trial route.
Defendants would also be eligible for up to two-thirds off jail sentences if they paid damages to the state.

The size of the damages would be set by the judge. The Democratic Party of the Left, the biggest force in Prodi's coalition, has called for guarantees that poor defendants would not be discriminated against.
Flick has denied that his proposals are a short-cut for Tangentopoli, saying his aim is to create "a criminal justice system that works better for everyone".
